title: Projects paid directly while their sponsor is also paid
question: Does the City pay a sponsored project in its own name as well as paying the organization that sponsors it?
finding: 1 City-paid organization says on its own return that it operated as a sponsored project of another City-paid organization: Housing Rights Committee of San Francisc (paid $8.2 million) under San Francisco Study Center Inc (paid $58.3 million). Of 127 project and trade names registered under the sponsors’ own business accounts, 0 appear as a City payee in their own right: by that test, nothing unusual. 9 more payees share only a suite-level address with a sponsor (SisterWeb at Heluna Health; San Francisco Youth Theatre at Community Initiatives; Chinatown Media and Arts Collaborative at Chinese For Affirmative Action; City Youth Now at Centers For Equity And Success, Inc); an address is a lead, not a link. The grant-chains file lists, pair by pair, the City-funded organizations that also receive onward grants from other City-funded organizations; those rows are not repeated here.
how: Three tests. First: returns in which the filer says it operated as a fiscally sponsored project of a named organization, with City payments to both. Second: the names tied to each self-declared sponsor in this project’s owner-groups (trade names on its business account, related organizations in a filing), checked against the payment file for payments in the name’s own right. Third: payees that share a suite-level address with a sponsor in the business registry, shown as address-only leads. City money is everything in the payment file under each name, fiscal 2019 to 2027 to date. Payments under $10,000 are ignored.
limits: A project paid both ways is not paid twice for the same thing unless the two payments fund the same work, which these files cannot show. A sponsored project can become its own corporation and start contracting directly, in which case both names are paid during the handover; and organizations that share a suite need have nothing else in common. A sponsored project that has no registration and no return of its own is invisible to all three tests: it is paid only through its sponsor. The City’s contract-approval notices, which often name a fiscal sponsor beside the contractor, are not read here; the places cross-check (screen fiscal-sponsors-named-on-notices) lists projects named that way that the City also pays in their own name, each a name match. What would settle it: each sponsor’s list of sponsored projects by year, set against the departments’ grant lists.
